summary:
Radiance is a prototype for context-aware radiation monitoring during human space missions. It brings together historical radiation measurements from NASA RadLab, solar proton observations and forecasts from NOAA SWPC and NASA CCMC, and solar-event records from NASA DONKI in a unified system.

A local FastAPI backend validates and stores scientific data in SQLite, allowing previously collected information to remain accessible without external internet connectivity. The web dashboard provides radiation trends, solar activity forecasts, a demonstrative 2D body map, and a pre-EVA evidence check that identifies missing, outdated, or incompatible measurements.

An independent browser-based wearable preview displays monitoring information and solar particle event notifications, with optional experimental vibration. Four synchronized simulation scenarios demonstrate how conditions evolve over time.

Radiance addresses the challenge by making complex space radiation information more accessible and easier to interpret. It separates real observations, scientific forecasts, and simulated data, supporting better-informed monitoring while acknowledging uncertainty. The prototype does not provide medical diagnoses or authorize spacewalks.
details:
Radiance — Context-Aware Radiation Monitoring

Project Overview

Radiance is a space radiation monitoring and decision-support prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

Our project aims to make complex space radiation information more accessible, understandable, and useful by combining scientific observations, solar activity forecasts, historical measurements, and contextual monitoring into a unified platform.

Radiance consists of two interconnected applications: a comprehensive web dashboard and an independent wearable interface designed to demonstrate how astronauts could access essential information during space missions.

Live Demonstrations

Radiance Web Dashboard:

https://radiance.luizsalomao.com.br/

Radiance Wearable:

https://wearable.luizsalomao.com.br/

Source Code and Technical Documentation:

https://github.com/marxz37/Mustach-NASA

How Does Radiance Work?

Radiance integrates publicly accessible scientific resources from NASA and NOAA, using a Python FastAPI backend to collect, validate, organize, and store information.

Our main scientific sources include:

  • NASA OSDR RadLab: Historical radiation measurements from instruments aboard the International Space Station, including absorbed dose rates and particle flux.
  • NOAA GOES/SWPC: Solar proton observations, solar event probabilities, and official space weather alerts.
  • NASA CCMC SEP Scoreboard: Scientific predictions of solar energetic particle events, including model-specific intensity, energy channels, and forecast timing.
  • NASA DONKI: Historical records of solar energetic particle events and related space weather information.

NASA's Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency radiation research also provide scientific foundations for the project's monitoring concepts.

The backend preserves the origin, measurement time, physical units, and scientific context of the collected data. An SQLite database provides persistent local storage, allowing previously collected information to remain accessible without external internet connectivity when the local backend is running.

Radiance separates information into three categories: real observations, scientific forecasts, and simulated data. This prevents fictional demonstration values from being presented as actual measurements.

Radiance Web Dashboard

The main application provides:

  • Radiation monitoring: Interactive graphs displaying radiation measurements and temporal trends.
  • Solar activity monitoring: Observed proton flux, solar event probabilities, forecast intensity, and event timing.
  • Radiation history: Historical records, accumulated dose calculations for compatible data, and interactive chart navigation.
  • Crew monitoring: Individual demonstration profiles with physiological indicators and radiation-related information.
  • Interactive 2D body map: A visual heatmap illustrating different exposure regions, with selectable anatomical areas.
  • EVA monitoring: A timer for extravehicular activities and demonstrative radiation exposure tracking.
  • Pre-EVA evidence verification: A system that evaluates whether relevant measurements are available, sufficiently recent, correctly associated with an activity, and suitable for review.

The anatomical heatmap and fictional crew information are demonstrative. They do not represent validated organ dosimetry or medical diagnoses.

Radiance Wearable

We also developed an independent browser-based wearable prototype that demonstrates how essential radiation information could be presented through a compact interface.

Its features include:

  • Radiation monitoring information and measurement status.
  • Visual indicators of available or missing personal exposure data.
  • Solar activity forecasts accessible through swipe navigation.
  • Notifications for relevant solar energetic particle events.
  • Optional experimental vibration for supported devices.
  • Communication with the same backend used by the web dashboard.

The wearable is currently a software prototype, not an application connected to a physical smartwatch or personal dosimeter.

Interactive Simulation

One of Radiance's main demonstration features is its synchronized simulation environment.

We developed four scenarios:

  1. Normal Conditions: Relatively stable fictional radiation readings.
  2. Solar Event Predicted: Increasing simulated solar event probability.
  3. Event in Progress: Changes in the simulated radiation environment.
  4. Recovery: Gradual reduction of simulated radiation levels.

Users can pause, resume, restart, or accelerate the simulation at 1×, 10×, or 60× speed.

Both the web dashboard and wearable obtain their scenario information from a shared FastAPI simulation engine, ensuring consistent demonstration behavior.

These scenarios make it possible to explore how the monitoring interface responds to changing conditions without requiring physical radiation sensors.

All simulation measurements and visual thresholds are fictional and explicitly distinguished from scientific observations.

Technologies Used

Radiance was developed using modern web technologies and a lightweight local data architecture.

Frontend and User Interface

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Lucide React
  • React Router

Scientific Visualization and Data Management

  • Apache ECharts
  • TanStack Query
  • Fetch API

Backend and Persistence

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Pydantic
  • SQLite

Testing and Development

  • Vitest
  • Pytest
  • Playwright
  • Git and GitHub
  • GitHub Actions

The project also supports English, Portuguese, and Spanish.

OpenAI Codex assisted with development, testing, and documentation. The project includes AI-generated fictional crew portraits. Scientific measurements and forecasts are obtained from their respective sources rather than generated by AI.

What Makes Radiance Creative?

Radiance goes beyond displaying isolated radiation measurements.

Its main innovation is combining scientific data, temporal context, data quality verification, and interactive visualization in a single monitoring experience.

Instead of simply showing a radiation value, the system considers the origin of the information, its timestamp, its physical unit, and whether it is appropriate for a specific monitoring context.

The pre-EVA evidence verification feature illustrates this approach by identifying missing, outdated, incompatible, or quality-flagged measurements before they are interpreted.

The combination of a full dashboard, compact wearable interface, synchronized simulations, and persistent historical data makes the system accessible across different monitoring situations.

Radiance also emphasizes scientific transparency: environmental measurements are not automatically interpreted as personal exposure, and solar particle forecasts are not treated as medical risk predictions.

Expected Benefits and Impact

The intended impact of Radiance is to improve how radiation-related information can be organized, visualized, and interpreted during human space missions.

Potential benefits include:

  • Making scientific radiation information easier to understand.
  • Improving awareness of changing solar activity conditions.
  • Supporting the review of available evidence before EVA operations.
  • Preserving historical records for subsequent analysis.
  • Demonstrating local access to previously collected data when external connectivity is unavailable.
  • Exploring how future wearable systems might deliver concise space weather notifications.
  • Providing an extensible foundation for research and future integration with validated personal dosimetry systems.

Radiance is designed as an educational and scientific research prototype that demonstrates a possible approach to context-aware monitoring.

It does not replace certified radiation instruments, provide medical diagnoses, predict an individual's probability of injury, or authorize spacewalks.

Design Considerations and Challenges

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific accuracy, usability, traceability, and reliability.

One important challenge was integrating information from different agencies and scientific instruments without confusing their physical meanings.

For example, absorbed dose rates, equivalent dose rates, integral proton flux, and differential proton flux represent different quantities and cannot be treated as interchangeable.

We also considered the limited availability of publicly accessible individual astronaut health data. Consequently, personal physiological indicators and anatomical exposure visualizations remain explicitly simulated.

Another important consideration was maintaining access to historical information without relying entirely on continuous external connectivity.

SQLite provides local persistence, while the API architecture separates scientific data collection from visualization.

Finally, we designed the user experience to prioritize the most relevant information, reduce unnecessary complexity, and provide both detailed monitoring and compact wearable presentation.

Conclusion

Radiance transforms distributed space radiation observations, scientific forecasts, and contextual information into an accessible monitoring experience.

By combining NASA and NOAA resources with interactive visualization, historical persistence, evidence verification, and wearable-oriented monitoring, our project demonstrates how scientific data can support more informed interpretation of radiation conditions during human space exploration.

Our goal is to contribute an extensible, scientifically transparent prototype that can support future research and inspire more accessible monitoring technologies for missions beyond Earth.
